extracted.intended_audience: Director of Central Intelligence / senior Intelligence Community leadership and policy officials
extracted.subtask_short: A-76 draft assessment for intelligence agencies
extracted.subtask_description: An internal Intelligence Community policy assessment of the draft OMB Circular A-76 (Performance of Commercial Activities), evaluating how the circular's rules on contracting vs in-house operations interact with protection of classified programs and sensitive intelligence material. Recommends community-wide positions and exemptions where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB A-76 prohibition on security/classification as justification for in-house operation
rubrics_metrics.description: "activities may not be justified for in-house operation on the basis that (1) there is a possibility of a strike by contract employees, [or] (2) the activity involves or supports a classified program."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit policy in the circular (unchanged in the draft) that prevents agencies from keeping activities in-house merely because they support classified programs or to guard against contractor strikes. The memo argues this policy is unacceptable for intelligence missions because it does not recognize security reasons as justification for government operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference to use private sector when practical, economical, and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Like the CIA, the National Security Agency relies on the private sector to provide goods and services whenever practical, economical, and appropriate.  We endorse the general policies espoused in OMB Circular A-76."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should favor contracting out where it is practical, economical, and appropriate. However, NSA/CIA note this preference must be balanced against security needs; endorsement of general policy is qualified by concerns about public exposure and flexibility under the A-76 procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that public exposure and lack of flexibility under A-76 compromise protection of sensitive intelligence material
rubrics_metrics.description: "the public exposure and lack of flexibility inherent in the program mandated by the circular would not permit us to adequately protect sensitive intelligence material."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the public nature of A-76 competitions (e.g., publicity, contractor access, procedural transparency) and rigid program procedures would increase risk to intelligence sources/methods. Example cited: DOE's proposed contracting of its all-source communications center — although consistent with A-76, it was unacceptable to users (including CIA), who threatened to discontinue electrical transmission of intelligence to DOE. Such operational impacts are a substantive reason to resist contracting in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for community-wide exemption/consistent Intelligence Community position
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everyone in the Intelligence Community shares the responsibility to protect intelligence sources and methods, and we should adopt a consistent community-wide position on what would or would not permit us to fulfill that responsibility.  Therefore, I enlist your support in seeking community-wide exemption from the circular."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy action recommended: the Intelligence Community should coordinate to seek an exemption from A-76 for activities where compliance would impair protection of intelligence sources/methods. This is both a substantive criterion (what would permit fulfilling the responsibility) and a procedural recommendation (seek exemption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional accommodations for unlimited contract operation of certain services (but no security exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the recent revision of the circular, provisions were made to accommodate a number of congressional concerns about unlimited contract operation of certain services, but no revision was made to the current policy that ... the activity involves or supports a classified program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although OMB revised the draft to address some congressional concerns about unbounded contracting-out, those revisions did not include recognition of security/classification as a valid basis to retain in-house operations. Agencies should note which Congressional-led exceptions exist and push for additional exceptions where security is implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may decline participation when circular conflicts with mission security (historical precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: On October 27, 1978, the Acting Deputy Director, CIA, sent a letter to Office of Management and Budget (OMB) describing cogently why CIA could not comply with the requirements of OMB Circular A-76.  OMB did not take exception to this letter, and CIA has not been participating in the A-76 program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical precedent: CIA formally notified OMB that it could not comply; OMB did not object and CIA opted out. Other intelligence entities, however, have been subject to the circular despite similar rationales. Agencies should consider formal, documented notification/refusal when compliance would violate security obligations, and coordinate IC positions to strengthen such refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational acceptability to users is a criterion for contracting decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Department of Energy's proposal last year to contract for the operation of its all-source communications center ... it was unacceptable to users of the communications center, including the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), who notified the Department of Energy that they would discontinue electrical transmission of intelligence to the Department of Energy if contractors operated the facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding to contract out a facility or service, assess whether the facility's users (internal or other agencies) will accept contractor operation. If contracting would cause users to withdraw critical inputs (e.g., intelligence transmission), that operational impact is a disqualifying factor for contracting under mission-protection grounds.
